title: Tom Sawyer Whitewashes the Fence
text:
It was a bright Saturday morning, and Tom Sawyer had been punished by his Aunt Polly. Instead of playing, he had to whitewash thirty yards of board fence nine feet high. He looked at the endless wall, felt the whole day being swallowed, and sat down in despair. He thought of paying someone to do it, but all his worldly wealth would not buy even half an hour of freedom.

Then he had an idea. When his friend Ben Rogers came by, eating an apple and pretending to be a steamboat, Tom kept painting with the absorbed care of an artist. Ben teased him about having to work. Tom said he didn't see it as work. Did a boy get a chance to whitewash a fence every day? He stepped back to study the effect of a stroke and added a touch here and there. Ben watched, and begged to be allowed to try. Tom refused: Aunt Polly was very particular about this fence, and not one boy in a thousand could do it right. In the end Ben gave him his apple for the privilege.

Other boys came by all day, and each one stayed to paint. By afternoon Tom had a kite, a dead rat on a string, twelve marbles and a pile of other treasures, and the fence had three coats of whitewash. Tom had discovered, Twain says, that to make someone want a thing, you only need to make it hard to get.
lesson: How a task is framed changes how people feel about doing it. If you want willing effort, show why the work is worth doing, but stay honest, because people resent a trick once they see it.
people: Tom Sawyer, Ben Rogers, Aunt Polly
source: Mark Twain, The Adventures of Tom Sawyer, Chapter 2
